Funding

Grant Readiness Guide

You don't have to be large to get funded — but you do have to be ready. This guide walks through the six things every neighborhood organization needs before they write a single word of a grant proposal.

See it in action: Roslindale Case Study →

1. Are You Grant-Ready? An Honest Self-Assessment

Most organizations that apply for grants before they're ready get rejected — not because their work isn't valuable, but because they can't demonstrate it yet. Before you write a single proposal, run through this readiness checklist honestly.

Organizational Foundation Checklist

501(c)(3) status or a fiscal sponsor — Most foundations require this. If you're not incorporated yet, find a fiscal sponsor (an existing nonprofit willing to administer grants on your behalf).
A board of directors with at least three members — Funders want governance accountability. A one-person organization rarely gets funded.
A checking account in the organization's name — Not a personal account. Most funders won't cut a check to an individual, even a well-intentioned one.
At least one completed project you can point to — Even a small success (a clean-up day, a community survey, a public meeting) shows you can execute. It doesn't need to be big.
A written mission statement and one-paragraph organizational summary — You'll use these in every proposal. Get them right before you start applying.
Documentation of community need — Data, survey results, or documented feedback from neighborhood outreach. This becomes your needs statement. (Outreach data helps enormously here.)
Prior grant experience — Not required for first-time applicants. Many funders specifically look for emerging organizations. Don't let inexperience stop you from applying to the right funders.

Not ready yet? Don't wait.

If you're missing something on this list, start working on it now — but don't wait for everything to be perfect before you start researching funders. The research takes months and you can do it in parallel with building your organizational infrastructure.

2. Finding the Right Funders

Applying to the wrong funders is the most common grant-writing mistake. A well-matched application to a small, well-aligned funder will almost always outperform a generic application to a large, misaligned foundation.

Where to Research

  • Candid (candid.org) — The largest database of U.S. foundations. Many libraries offer free access. Search by geography, focus area, and giving size.
  • 990 filings on ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer — Every foundation files a Form 990-PF annually, which lists every grant they made. This is the most reliable research tool available.
  • Your own community — Who funded similar projects nearby? Ask peer organizations. Their 990s are public too.
  • Local community foundations — Almost every region has a community foundation that funds neighborhood-level work. These are often your best first grants.
  • Government sources — CDBG (Community Development Block Grant) funds flow through cities and counties and specifically target neighborhood organizations.

What to Look For in a Funder

Criteria What to Find Red Flags
Geographic focus Explicitly funds your city, county, or neighborhood National funder with no local history; different state
Issue alignment Their priority areas match what you do Vague "community" focus with no specifics; mission drift in recent 990s
Typical grant size Their average grant is within range of what you need You're asking for 10x their typical grant; or you're asking for far less than their minimum
Eligibility They fund 501(c)(3) orgs or accept fiscal sponsorship They only fund established nonprofits with 5+ year track records
Recent grantees You know or can connect with past grantees No grantees like you in size, geography, or issue area

3. Building Your Case

Before you write a proposal, you need to be able to answer four questions clearly. If you can't answer all four, your proposal will be weak regardless of how well it's written.

Question 1: What is the problem?

Describe the specific, documented need in your community. Use data when you have it (census data, survey results, city reports), but also use human-scale descriptions. "14% of households in our ZIP code are food-insecure" is strong data. "Our outreach team spoke with 87 families who reported skipping meals in the past month" is stronger combined with it.

Question 2: Who else is working on it?

Funders want to know you're not duplicating existing services. Name the other organizations working on related issues in your community — and explain clearly what gap your organization fills that they don't.

Question 3: What will you do, specifically?

Avoid vague language like "raise awareness" or "support the community." Be specific: "We will host six community meetings over three months, each attended by 30–50 residents, resulting in a written neighborhood plan to be submitted to the city planning department by March 15th."

Question 4: How will you know it worked?

This is your evaluation plan. It doesn't need to be sophisticated — it needs to be honest. List the outcomes you expect (not activities), and describe how you'll measure each one. A simple before/after survey, attendance counts, and documented decisions are often enough for neighborhood-scale grants.

"The strongest proposals we fund don't necessarily have the most polished writing. They're the ones where we can tell the people writing them actually know the neighborhood and have a clear plan."

— Program Officer, regional community foundation (from a Civic Signal interview)

4. Elements of a Strong Proposal

Most grant proposals — regardless of funder — ask for the same basic information, organized in similar ways. Here's what each section needs to accomplish.

Executive Summary (1 paragraph)

State who you are, what you're asking for, what it will fund, and what the outcome will be. Write this last, after all other sections are done. Funders often read only this and the budget before deciding whether to keep reading.

Organizational Background (1–2 paragraphs)

Brief history, mission, key accomplishments, governance structure. Lead with what you've done, not who you are. Funders are investing in capacity — show them you have it.

Statement of Need (2–3 paragraphs)

Document the community need with data and human detail. Cite sources. Reference your outreach data if you have it — showing that you went door-to-door and heard directly from residents is more compelling than a census table alone.

Project Description (3–5 paragraphs)

What will you do, when, and who's responsible? Include a timeline with milestones. Be specific about activities, participants, and locations. If you're collaborating with other organizations, name them and describe each party's role.

Evaluation Plan (1–2 paragraphs)

List your outcomes (changes, not activities) and describe how you'll measure each. Keep it honest — funders don't expect academic rigor from neighborhood organizations, but they do expect you to know the difference between an output (30 people attended) and an outcome (20 of those people became active members and attended all subsequent meetings).

Budget

Line-item budgets organized by category (Personnel, Fringe/Benefits, Supplies, Printing, Consultant Fees, Indirect Costs). Every line needs to be justified. Include in-kind contributions (donated space, volunteer labor) — these show that your community has skin in the game and that the grant is leveraging local resources, not replacing them.

Common Proposal Mistakes

Don't describe your activities as outcomes. "We will host six meetings" is an activity. "Residents will develop a written plan submitted to the city" is an outcome. Don't apply for more than you need. Don't leave budget lines unexplained. Don't submit a generic proposal — funders can tell when the "community" described in your needs statement is somewhere else.

5. Building Funder Relationships

Grants are not lotteries. They're relationships. The organizations that get funded reliably — year after year — treat funders as partners, not ATMs.

Before You Apply

If the funder allows it, call or email before submitting. Introduce yourself briefly, ask if your project is a good fit, and ask what they'd want to see emphasized. This is not begging — it's what sophisticated grant-seekers do. A program officer who has already talked with you is far more likely to champion your proposal.

After You Apply

Thank them promptly, and keep them in the loop with brief updates even if they haven't responded yet. If you do something newsworthy — a big community event, a policy win, an award — let them know. You're building a relationship with a person who will eventually move on to another job and bring their opinion of your organization with them.

After You're Funded

Report on time, every time. Send interim and final reports that are honest about what went differently than planned — funders expect reality, not perfection. Acknowledge the funder publicly (in meeting handouts, your newsletter, meeting agendas) — this is how you stay fundable long-term.

When You're Rejected

Ask for feedback. Not all funders will provide it, but some will — and it's invaluable. Thank them anyway. Many funded organizations were rejected their first time applying to a funder, then tried again the following year with a stronger proposal built on the feedback they received.

6. Your Grant Calendar Template

Organizations that apply for grants on an ad-hoc basis almost always lose to organizations that plan their grant activity in advance. A grant calendar shows you — at a glance — what you're working on, what's due, and what's coming up in the next cycle.

Below is a template you can adapt to your year. Most foundation cycles run annually or biannually; community foundations often have quarterly rounds. Build your calendar around the deadlines of your target funders.

Q1 · Jan–Mar
Research Identify 6–10 new prospective funders from 990 research; update existing list
Relationship Reach out to 2–3 program officers for introductory calls
Due dates Note all spring deadlines from your prospective funder list
Reporting File year-end reports for grants received last calendar year
Q2 · Apr–Jun
Apply Submit spring cycle proposals; track submissions in a log
Stewardship Host site visits from interested funders; send project updates
Plan ahead Identify fall deadlines; start drafting narratives for new funders
Board Present grant pipeline to board; note any funding gaps
Q3 · Jul–Sep
Awards Spring decisions arrive; acknowledge awards and begin agreements
Apply Submit fall cycle proposals; tailor narratives per funder
Interim reports File mid-year progress reports for active grants
Research Identify any new funders that emerged from summer convenings
Q4 · Oct–Dec
Awards Fall decisions arrive; plan budget accordingly
Stewardship Year-end funder appreciation; thank-you letters, annual report
Plan Draft next year's grant calendar; review this year's outcomes data
Renew Reach out to current funders about renewal timing and priorities

See it in action

The Roslindale Community Garden Network raised $85,000 over 18 months using a grant strategy that closely mirrors this framework — starting with a community foundation and expanding from there. Read the full case study →

Quick Reference

Typical grant amounts

Community foundations: $1,000–$25,000
CDBG: $5,000–$50,000
State/regional: $10,000–$100,000+

Turnaround time

Application to decision: 3–6 months
Award to first payment: 1–3 months
Plan for 6–9 months total
